title: Sudden left leg weakness in a man with atrial fibrillation
desc: This station involves a time-critical focused history and neurological examination of a 65-year-old man with sudden weakness and numbness of the left leg and urinary incontinence after two earlier brief episodes. The candidate then interprets his observations, bloods, ECG and code stroke CT, separates stroke from TIA, localises the lesion to the anterior cerebral artery territory, works through reperfusion while he is taking apixaban, and gives secondary prevention and safety netting.
focus: Acute focal weakness: recognising stroke, localising an anterior cerebral artery syndrome and deciding on reperfusion in a patient on apixaban
diagnosis: Acute ischaemic stroke, right anterior cerebral artery territory
stem: You are the junior medical officer in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Mr Dominic Rodriguez, a 65-year-old telemarketer, has been brought in by his wife because his left leg suddenly became weak this morning. He was triaged as category 2. He is lying on a trolley in an acute bay. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Rodriguez and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Start any immediate management you think he needs as you go (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, blood results, ECG and CT report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Dominic Rodriguez, aged 65. You work from home as a telemarketer. You are lying on an ED trolley and cannot move your left leg. You are frightened but clear-headed and you speak normally. Your wife brought you in and is in the waiting room. Give the history below only when asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining. The nurse gives the observations, a bedside glucose and a bladder scan result if asked.

Opening line: "Hey doc, I suddenly felt weakness in my leg about 2 hours ago and am a bit worried about this, so my wife brought me in just then."

If asked to say more: "I have also been wetting my pants."

The weakness (give only when asked)

  • It came on suddenly at about 9:30 this morning while you were walking around your bedroom. You were completely well just before.
  • It is your left leg, all the way up to the hip. It is only one side and it has not spread anywhere else.
  • "It feels heavy and dead. I can't lift it at all. I also don't feel anything."
  • "It's really scaring me. I can't walk on my left leg at all. I fell over when it suddenly came on, but I was lucky I was just in my bedroom at the time. I couldn't even put my shoes and socks on to come to emergency. My wife had to do it for me."
  • If asked about the fall: you went down onto the carpet and were not hurt. You did not hit your head.
  • It has been there constantly since it started, and it might be slowly getting a bit worse. Nothing makes it better or worse.
  • There were no palpitations beforehand and no injury before it started.

Earlier episodes (only if asked whether this has happened before)

  • A few weeks ago, and again about a month ago, your left leg suddenly went weak, came and went, and was back to normal after about 10 minutes each time.
  • You did not see a doctor or tell anyone because it went away so quickly.

Numbness

  • No feeling in the left leg. No tingling and no pain. It started at the same time as the weakness. The earlier episodes had the same numbness.

Wetting yourself

  • You have wet yourself twice in the last 2 hours, without warning. It started with everything else.
  • The urine looks normal: no blood, froth or pus. No burning. You can pass urine and do not feel your bladder is full. Bowels normal.

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • No weakness, numbness or droop of the face or arms. No trouble finding words, understanding or slurred speech. No one has said you are ignoring your left side.
  • No change in your vision, no double vision, no dizziness or spinning, no nausea, no memory problems.
  • No headache, no vomiting, no drowsiness, no neck stiffness.
  • No back pain, no pain shooting down the legs, no numbness around the bottom or genitals.
  • No fits, jerking, tongue biting or blackout.
  • You ate breakfast at 8 am. No sweating, shaking or feeling of a "hypo".
  • No chest pain and no palpitations. You get puffed walking, but that has not changed. No swollen ankles, no breathlessness lying flat or waking breathless.
  • No leg pain or swelling.
  • No weight loss, night sweats, loss of appetite, lumps or cough. No fever, sore throat or cold symptoms.

Past medical history

  • Type 2 diabetes for 10 years.
  • Atrial fibrillation diagnosed a year ago.
  • High blood pressure for 6 years. High cholesterol.
  • Reflux (GORD) for 10 years.
  • A heart attack 5 years ago, treated with a stent.

Medications

  • Perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin at night, metformin twice daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, and fish oil.
  • Apixaban 5 mg twice a day. Only if asked how you take it: "To be honest I forget it a fair bit." Only if asked when you last took it: you took a tablet with dinner at about 7 pm last night and forgot this morning's dose.
  • Vaccinations up to date.

Allergies

  • Penicillin: a bad rash.
  • Nuts: anaphylaxis.

Family history

  • Your mother died of a sudden cardiac arrest at 40.
  • Your father died of a heart attack at 78.
  • Your 4 sisters and 2 brothers all have type 2 diabetes. You have no children.

Social history

  • You smoke a pack a day and have done for about 15 years.
  • Social drinker, a few drinks on weekends.
  • Occasional cocaine at parties, but not in the last few weeks. Admit this only if asked directly and without judgement.
  • You work from home on the phones as a telemarketer. Little exercise, and you get puffed easily. Fast food about 5 times a week.
  • You live with your wife. She does the chores and looks after you. Before today you could walk around the house and local shops without help.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • You wonder if it is a stroke but hope it is a pinched nerve.
  • You are scared you will never walk again and your wife will have to do everything for you.
  • You have read that COVID causes clots, and you are worried you might have COVID.
  • You want them to "fix it today".

During the station

  • About halfway through, say: "Could I get a glass of water? My mouth's really dry." If the candidate explains why you should not drink yet, accept it. If they offer water or tablets by mouth without a swallow check, the examiner notes it.
  • Ask once: "Is this a stroke, doc?"
  • If the candidate asks for a code stroke, the stroke team or an urgent CT, the nurse says: "Code stroke called. The stroke registrar is on the way and CT is ready for him as soon as you've finished." Do not stop the station.
  • If the candidate has not established the time of onset or asked for urgent help by halfway, the nurse asks: "Is there anything you want me to organise?"

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: alert, GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6). Central obesity, weight 102 kg. Wet trousers. No injury from the fall, no scalp or head wound.
  • Vital signs: RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 158/92, HR 92 irregularly irregular, temperature 36.8 °C, pain 0/10. Bedside glucose 8.4 mmol/L.
  • Cardiovascular: irregularly irregular pulse. Heart sounds dual with no murmur. No carotid bruits. JVP not raised. No ankle oedema. Calves soft and non-tender.
  • Chest: clear.
  • Speech and higher function: fluent speech with normal comprehension, naming and repetition. No dysarthria. Oriented. No visual or sensory inattention on either side.
  • Cranial nerves: visual fields full to confrontation. Pupils equal and reactive. Eye movements full, no nystagmus. Face symmetrical, with normal forehead and lower face movement. Normal facial sensation, palate and tongue.
  • Upper limbs: normal tone, power 5/5 throughout on both sides, including shoulder abduction. No pronator drift. Reflexes normal and symmetrical. Normal sensation. Finger-nose normal.
  • Lower limbs, left: reduced tone. Hip flexion 1/5 (a flicker). Hip extension, knee and ankle 0/5. Knee and ankle reflexes present, slightly reduced compared with the right. Plantar extensor (upgoing). Light touch, pinprick, vibration and joint position sense absent from the foot to the groin.
  • Lower limbs, right: normal tone, power 5/5, normal reflexes, plantar flexor, normal sensation.
  • Trunk and saddle: no sensory level on the trunk. Perianal and saddle sensation intact.
  • Back: no spinal tenderness or deformity.
  • Abdomen and bladder: soft, bladder not palpable. Bladder scan if asked: 60 mL after he was changed. If a PR is offered: normal anal tone and perianal sensation.
  • Gait: unable to stand on the left leg (do not test).
  • NIHSS if asked: 5 (left leg motor 3, sensory 2, all other items 0).

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms the patient's identity, and asks permission before examining.
Acknowledges his fear with empathy, uses plain language, explains what is happening and why he cannot drink yet, and keeps the history focused because the presentation is time-critical.
History
Characterises the weakness:

kids.x: Establishes the exact time of onset (sudden, about 9:30 am while walking, well just before) as the last known well time
Distribution and severity: left leg up to the hip only, cannot lift it or walk, constant and not spreading
Numbness of the same leg, starting at the same time, with no tingling or pain
The fall at onset, with no injury and no head strike

check.x: Explores the incontinence: twice in 2 hours since the onset, no warning, normal-looking urine, no dysuria, and no feeling of retention.
Asks whether this has happened before and elicits two earlier episodes of left leg weakness lasting about 10 minutes each over the past month, which he did not report.
Screens for features of other vascular territories and of raised intracranial pressure:

kids.x: Middle cerebral artery: face or arm weakness, speech or language difficulty, neglect, visual field loss
Posterior circulation: visual disturbance, vertigo, nausea, memory problems
Raised intracranial pressure or haemorrhage: headache, vomiting, drowsiness

check.x: Screens for mimics and spinal causes: hypoglycaemia symptoms and meals, seizure, back or radicular pain, saddle numbness and urinary retention, fever or infective symptoms, and cancer symptoms.
Asks about cardiac symptoms: palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, heart failure symptoms, and calf pain or swelling.
Takes the past history (AF, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, MI with a stent, GORD) and allergies with the reactions (penicillin rash, nut anaphylaxis).
Asks about apixaban adherence and the time of the last dose (often forgets it, last dose about 7 pm last night, missed this morning), and notes the aspirin.
Asks about family history of cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
Takes the social history:

kids.x: Smoking (a pack a day for 15 years, about 15 pack-years), alcohol, and cocaine use, asked without judgement
Diet, exercise, work from home, lives with his wife who cares for him, and independent walking before today

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations, including his fear of not walking again and his worry about COVID.
Examination
Asks for a bedside blood glucose straight away to exclude hypoglycaemia (8.4 mmol/L).
General and cardiovascular examination: GCS, injuries from the fall, an irregularly irregular pulse, BP, heart sounds and carotid bruits.
Examines speech, visual fields, inattention, the cranial nerves and both arms (tone, power, pronator drift, reflexes, coordination), finding them normal, so the face and arm are spared.
Examines both legs and identifies an acute central (UMN) deficit of the left leg, with an extensor plantar despite reduced tone:

kids.x: Tone and power: reduced tone, hip flexion 1/5 and 0/5 distally on the left, normal on the right
Reflexes and plantars: left plantar extensor
Sensation in all modalities lost from foot to groin on the left, with no sensory level on the trunk

check.x: Looks for a spinal cause: palpates the spine, tests saddle sensation, and checks for a palpable bladder or asks for a bladder scan (PR not required).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: all in the white zone with AF at a controlled rate and BP 158/92, below 185/110. States that a white zone chart does not make him safe, because a new focal deficit within hours of onset is a code stroke regardless of the chart.

Interprets the bloods: glucose 8.6 excludes hypoglycaemia as a mimic, platelets and renal function are normal, and a normal INR and APTT do not exclude apixaban effect, so the apixaban level is needed before any thrombolysis decision.
Interprets the ECG as atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate and no acute ischaemic change, which makes a cardioembolic source likely.
Interprets the CT:

kids.x: Non-contrast CT shows no intracranial haemorrhage or mass
CT angiogram shows an occlusion of the right A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery
CT perfusion shows a small core with a much larger penumbra in the right ACA territory: salvageable tissue

check.x: States that this is a stroke, not a TIA: the deficit is still present at 2 to 3 hours and imaging shows ischaemia. Names the two earlier 10-minute episodes as TIAs.

Localises the stroke to the right anterior cerebral artery territory, giving contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss with urinary incontinence. Explains it is not MCA (no face or arm weakness, aphasia, neglect or hemianopia), not PCA (no visual field loss) and not posterior circulation (no vertigo, nausea, diplopia or ataxia).
Gives the differentials with a feature against each: intracerebral haemorrhage, hypoglycaemia, spinal cord or cauda equina compression, Todd's paresis after a seizure, and tumour or abscess.
Management
In Part 1, once the onset time is known, activates a code stroke or calls the stroke team and requests an urgent non-contrast CT brain with CT angiography and perfusion.

States that he is within the thrombolysis window, but apixaban taken within 48 hours (last dose about 7 pm last night) contraindicates thrombolysis unless the apixaban level shows no significant drug effect under the local protocol. Leaves the decision to the stroke consultant.

Urgently discusses with the stroke and neurointervention team whether clot retrieval is appropriate, recognising that an A2 occlusion is a medium vessel occlusion where routine clot retrieval has not shown benefit (ESCAPE-MeVO, DISTAL 2025) and is decided case by case; states that anticoagulation does not by itself rule it out.
Blood pressure: does not lower it routinely, and keeps it below 185/110 before and 180/105 after any reperfusion therapy.

Keeps him nil by mouth, including tablets, until a swallow screen is passed. Withholds apixaban and aspirin until the stroke team decides. Monitors glucose and temperature, and gives no routine oxygen while SpO2 is normal.

Admits him to the stroke unit with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech pathology. Uses intermittent pneumatic compression for VTE prevention while he is immobile, assesses falls and pressure risk, and manages continence without a routine catheter.
Explains in plain words that the clot most likely came from his AF, and names his main modifiable risk factors (missed apixaban, smoking, BP, diabetes, cholesterol).
Explains that missed apixaban doses left his AF unprotected, and addresses adherence: twice-daily dosing, reminders or a dose administration aid, and pharmacist review.

Outlines secondary prevention: anticoagulation restarted when the stroke team advises, statin, BP and diabetes control, quitting smoking with support and stopping cocaine, and diet and exercise. Answers the COVID worry: the test is negative and the AF explains the clot.
Safety netting

Sets escalation triggers for the nurses: any new weakness of the face or arm, speech change, drowsiness or a fall in GCS, new headache or vomiting, BP above the stroke team's limits, fever, or coughing or choking with oral intake.

Tells Dominic and his wife in plain words that a drooping face, a weak arm or leg, or trouble speaking (FAST) means calling 000 straight away, even if it gets better within minutes, as the earlier episodes did.
Mentions no driving for at least 4 weeks and GP and stroke clinic follow-up.

part2.lead: Here are his observations since arrival, his blood results, his ECG and the code stroke CT report.
part2.patient:
• If the candidate explains that the clot-busting drug cannot be given because of his apixaban, ask: "So there's nothing you can do to fix it?" (A good answer explains that the stroke team is deciding whether any clot treatment is safe and helpful, and that stroke unit care and rehabilitation improve recovery.)
  • When the candidate answers your question about why this happened, ask: "Is this because of COVID?" and then "Will I walk again?"
  • If the candidate uses jargon ("anterior cerebral artery", "anticoagulant"), say: "Sorry, what does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations since arrival
handover.result: Room air throughout. GCS 15 and pupils equal and reactive at each check. Left leg power unchanged.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 16 to 18, SpO2 96 to 97% on room air, BP 154 to 158 systolic, HR 88 to 96 irregular, temperature 36.8 to 37.0 °C, alert. Every value is in the white zone at all three times, and the bedside glucose of 8.4 mmol/L excludes hypoglycaemia (mildly raised, non-fasting, in a known diabetic).
  • Meaning: the chart triggers no clinical review or rapid response. AF has a controlled rate, and BP is mildly raised but below the 185/110 that would have to be met before thrombolysis. He is not hypoxic or febrile, and his neurology is stable, not worsening.
  • Changes: a white zone chart does not make this safe. A new focal deficit within hours of onset is a code stroke on its own. He needs neuro observations, no routine oxygen, no routine BP lowering, and escalation for any change in neurology, headache or vomiting.

rows.note: Returned from CT; left leg unchanged
Neuro obs: GCS 15, pupils equal, left leg unchanged

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Venous samples collected 11:40. Apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa level requested at 11:40: result pending.
handover.model:
• Read: FBC normal, with platelets 236. Electrolytes and renal function normal (creatinine 92, eGFR 74). Venous glucose 8.6, mildly raised in a known diabetic. INR 1.1 and APTT 33 are normal. hs-troponin I 9 is normal. SARS-CoV-2 PCR not detected. The apixaban level is pending.
  • Meaning: hypoglycaemia is excluded as a mimic. Platelets are normal (thrombocytopenia below 100 would be a separate thrombolysis contraindication), and renal function is normal, so apixaban is not expected to accumulate. A normal INR and APTT do not exclude a clinically important apixaban effect, so his last dose at about 7 pm last night still counts. The troponin shows no concurrent MI, and the negative PCR answers his COVID worry.
  • Changes: thrombolysis is not given on the strength of normal routine coagulation results. The stroke team decides with the apixaban level and the local protocol. Glucose is monitored and treated if high.

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG at 11:30 (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV)

  • Rate: ventricular rate about 90/min.
  • Rhythm: irregularly irregular. No P waves, with a fine fibrillatory baseline: atrial fibrillation.
  • Axis: normal, about +40°.
  • PR interval: not measurable.
  • QRS duration: 94 ms.
  • QTc: 438 ms.
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression in any lead. T waves normal.
  • Other: no pathological Q waves, no bundle branch block, no LVH by voltage criteria.
  • Comparison: unchanged from the cardiology clinic ECG of last year, which also showed atrial fibrillation.
handover.model:
• Read: atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate of about 90, normal axis and intervals, no acute ST or T change, unchanged from last year.
  • Meaning: this is his known AF, and with recently missed apixaban doses it is the most likely source of a cardioembolic stroke. There is no acute coronary syndrome.
  • Changes: no rate control is needed now. Cardiac monitoring continues, and the long-term plan is reliable anticoagulation, restarted when the stroke team advises.

handover.label: Code stroke CT report
handover.result:
Examination: CT brain without contrast, followed by CT angiography (aortic arch to vertex) and CT perfusion after IV contrast, 11:50.

Clinical details: 65-year-old man. Sudden left leg weakness and numbness from 09:30 with urinary incontinence. AF on apixaban. Code stroke.

Findings:

  • Non-contrast CT brain: no intracranial haemorrhage. Possible subtle loss of grey-white differentiation in the right paracentral lobule. No established infarct. No mass, no midline shift, ventricles and sulci normal for age. Mild periventricular white matter low density in keeping with small vessel change.
  • CT angiogram: abrupt occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery in the proximal A2 segment, just beyond the anterior communicating artery, with reduced opacification of the distal right pericallosal and callosomarginal branches. Left ACA, both middle cerebral arteries, both posterior cerebral arteries and the basilar artery are patent. Mild calcified plaque at both carotid bifurcations without significant stenosis (less than 50%). Vertebral arteries normal. No aneurysm.
  • CT perfusion: perfusion deficit (Tmax above 6 seconds) of 42 mL in the right ACA territory (medial frontal and parietal lobes, including the paracentral lobule). Core (relative CBF below 30%) 6 mL. Mismatch volume 36 mL, mismatch ratio 7.

Conclusion: acute right anterior cerebral artery territory ischaemia from a proximal right A2 occlusion, with a small core and a large area of potentially salvageable tissue. No haemorrhage.
handover.model:
• Read: no haemorrhage or mass on the non-contrast scan, with only a subtle early change in the right paracentral lobule. The CTA shows a right A2 occlusion with all other major vessels patent and no significant carotid stenosis. CTP shows a 6 mL core within a 42 mL perfusion deficit, a large mismatch.
  • Meaning: this confirms an acute ischaemic stroke in the right ACA territory, matching the left leg weakness, sensory loss and incontinence. Haemorrhage, tumour and abscess are excluded, and the lack of carotid stenosis fits an embolus from the heart. Most of the affected tissue can still be saved.
  • Changes: urgent stroke team review; clot retrieval for a medium vessel A2 occlusion is not routine and is decided case by case. Thrombolysis depends on the apixaban level. No carotid intervention is needed.

ask: The stroke registrar has just arrived. Please give an ISBAR handover of Dominic Rodriguez, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Dominic now, here in the emergency department.
Dominic asks you, "Why did this happen to me, and what do I need to do so it doesn't happen again?" Please answer him.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED JMO; Dominic Rodriguez, 65.
  • Situation: sudden left leg weakness, numbness and incontinence since 09:30, about 3 hours; acute right ACA stroke with a right A2 occlusion; on apixaban.
  • Background: two 10-minute left leg TIAs this month; AF, hypertension, T2DM, high cholesterol, MI with stent; apixaban often missed, last dose 7 pm last night; aspirin; smoker, cocaine; penicillin and nut allergy.
  • Assessment: obs white zone, AF about 90, BP 158/92; glucose 8.4, no hypoglycaemia; left leg 1/5 at hip, 0/5 distally, sensory loss, upgoing plantar, face and arm spared, NIHSS 5; ECG AF only; normal INR/APTT do not exclude apixaban, level pending; CT no bleed, A2 occlusion, core 6 mL, mismatch 36 mL.
  • Recommendation: please assess now for the reperfusion decision; stroke unit bed.

Acute ischaemic stroke, right ACA territory, cardioembolic from AF: sudden contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss with incontinence, face and arm spared; still present after more than an hour, with A2 occlusion and perfusion deficit, so stroke not TIA; earlier 10-minute episodes were TIAs; AF with missed apixaban.

  • Intracerebral haemorrhage (apixaban, aspirin, hypertension): no headache or vomiting, excluded on CT.
  • Hypoglycaemia (diabetic): glucose 8.4.
  • Spinal cord or cauda equina compression: no back pain, saddle sensation intact, no retention, upgoing plantar, no sensory level.
  • Todd's paresis: no seizure.
  • Tumour or abscess: sudden onset, afebrile, no mass on CT.

1. Code stroke already called; stroke registrar at the bedside now; cardiac and neuro monitoring.
  2. Thrombolysis: within 4.5 h, but apixaban within 48 h contraindicates it unless the apixaban level shows no significant effect under the local protocol; normal INR/APTT do not clear it; stroke consultant decides.
  3. Clot retrieval: A2 is a medium vessel occlusion where routine clot retrieval has not shown benefit (ESCAPE-MeVO, DISTAL 2025); urgent case-by-case discussion with stroke and neurointervention; apixaban does not by itself exclude it.
  4. BP: no routine lowering; below 185/110 before and 180/105 after reperfusion.
  5. Nil by mouth, including tablets, until a swallow screen; withhold apixaban and aspirin; glucose and temperature monitoring; no routine oxygen.
  6. Stroke unit; physiotherapy, OT, speech pathology; intermittent pneumatic compression; falls, pressure and continence care.
  7. Nurse escalation: new face or arm weakness, speech change, drowsiness, headache, vomiting.
  8. Update Dominic and his wife.

• Why: a clot most likely formed in the irregular heart rhythm (AF) and blocked a brain artery supplying the leg. Missed apixaban doses left him unprotected. The earlier brief episodes were warnings (TIAs).
  • Main risk factors he can change: missed apixaban, smoking, high BP, diabetes, cholesterol.
  • Prevention: take apixaban twice daily every day (reminders, a dose administration aid, pharmacist), restarted when the stroke team advises; statin, BP and diabetes control; quit smoking with support and stop cocaine; diet, exercise.
  • COVID: test negative; AF explains it.
  • Walking: too early to say; rehabilitation helps many people.
  • Safety net: FAST signs mean call 000 at once, even if they settle; no driving for at least 4 weeks; GP and stroke clinic follow-up.

ddx.dx: Acute ischaemic stroke in the right anterior cerebral artery territory, cardioembolic from atrial fibrillation
ddx.for: Sudden left leg weakness and sensory loss with urinary incontinence, sparing the face and arm, still present at 2 hours after two 10-minute TIAs, in AF with missed apixaban doses, with a right A2 occlusion and ACA perfusion deficit on CT.
He takes apixaban and aspirin together and has hypertension.
ddx.against: No headache, vomiting or drowsiness, and the non-contrast CT shows no haemorrhage.

ddx.for: He has type 2 diabetes on metformin.
ddx.against: He ate breakfast, has no adrenergic symptoms, and his bedside glucose is 8.4 mmol/L.

ddx.dx: Spinal cord or cauda equina compression
ddx.for: He has leg weakness with sensory loss and urinary incontinence.
ddx.against: Only one leg is affected, with no back or radicular pain, intact saddle sensation, no retention on bladder scan, no sensory level, and an upgoing plantar with a vascular cause shown on CT.

ddx.dx: Todd's paresis after an unwitnessed seizure
ddx.for: He has a sudden focal deficit with incontinence and fell at onset.
ddx.against: He remembers the onset clearly with no blackout, jerking or tongue biting, and the deficit has not improved over 3 hours.

ddx.for: A focal deficit can come from a mass lesion, and he is a 65-year-old smoker.
ddx.against: The onset was abrupt, with no headache, fever, weight loss or night sweats, and CT shows no mass.

guide:
This is an acute station. The candidate should find the onset time early and ask for urgent help. The nurse confirms a code stroke when it is called; do not stop Part 1 for the CT. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Tick item 31 only if the code stroke or an urgent stroke team call with CT is requested during Part 1. If the candidate asks for bloods, an ECG or CT results in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. Dominic asks for water about halfway through; credit item 35 in Part 2 only from the answer to the management question, but note an unsafe offer of water or tablets.

In Part 2, hand over the observations, bloods, ECG and CT report together, then ask the four questions in order. Read Dominic's question aloud for the fourth. The person playing Dominic adds his follow-up questions from the Part 2 script.

A high-performing candidate fixes the time of onset and the last apixaban dose, elicits the earlier TIAs, checks the glucose, screens other territories and spinal causes, and finds an upper motor neurone left leg deficit with the face and arm spared. In Part 2 they call it a stroke, not a TIA, and localise it to the right ACA. They read the CT as an A2 occlusion with salvageable tissue and no bleed. They explain that normal routine coagulation does not exclude apixaban, so thrombolysis depends on the drug level and the stroke consultant, and that clot retrieval for this medium vessel occlusion is not routine and is discussed urgently with the stroke team case by case. They keep him nil by mouth until a swallow screen, avoid routine BP lowering, and give a clear, non-judgemental explanation of his risk factors and adherence.

A borderline candidate takes a broad history without the onset time or the apixaban timing, misses the earlier episodes, or examines only the legs. They may call it MCA or a TIA, or plan thrombolysis because the INR is normal. Their plan may be "admit and refer to neurology" without urgency, and their safety netting is vague.
explain:
Diagnosis: a right anterior cerebral artery stroke

Dominic has a sudden, persisting deficit of the left leg (weakness and loss of all sensory modalities to the groin) with urinary incontinence. His face, arm, speech, vision and attention are spared. This pattern localises to the medial surface of the right hemisphere: the paracentral lobule holds the leg area of the motor and sensory cortex and the cortical centre for bladder control. That is the territory of the right anterior cerebral artery. The CT angiogram confirms a proximal A2 occlusion. Isolated ACA infarcts are uncommon, about 2% of ischaemic strokes, because the anterior communicating artery usually lets the other ACA supply the territory. A2 occlusions lie beyond the anterior communicating artery, so this protection is lost.

Typical ACA features are contralateral leg weakness more than arm (the shoulder may be involved), with the face and hand spared; contralateral leg sensory loss; urinary incontinence; abulia (reduced drive and slowed responses); limb apraxia; and sometimes speech disturbance. Dominic's dense leg weakness stopped him walking or putting on his shoes and socks. In the first hours after a stroke the limb is often flaccid with reduced reflexes (cerebral shock); the extensor plantar is the reliable UMN sign, and spasticity develops over days. An MCA stroke would affect the face and arm more than the leg, and would cause aphasia (dominant side), neglect (non-dominant side) or a hemianopia. A PCA stroke would cause a visual field defect, and posterior circulation strokes cause vertigo, nausea, ataxia or memory problems. In older patients with hypotension or carotid stenosis, ACA/MCA watershed infarcts can give a proximal "man in a barrel" pattern instead.

Stroke or TIA?

Most TIAs resolve within an hour. Under the current tissue-based definition, a TIA is a transient deficit without infarction on imaging. Dominic's deficit is still present at 2 to 3 hours and imaging shows ischaemia, so this is a stroke. His two 10-minute episodes of left leg weakness over the previous month were TIAs in the same territory. He did not report them. A TIA is a medical emergency and patients should be taught to call 000 even when symptoms settle.

The cause and his risk factors

AF with missed doses of apixaban is the most likely embolic source. The CTA shows no significant carotid stenosis. His other risk factors are male sex, age 65, a family history of early cardiac death, previous TIAs, hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia, coronary disease, smoking (about 15 pack-years), cocaine use, likely obesity, a poor diet and little exercise. His worry about COVID is reasonable to raise, but he has no infective symptoms and the PCR is negative.

Mimics and the dangerous alternatives

Check glucose in every suspected stroke, because hypoglycaemia mimics it, especially in a diabetic. Intracerebral haemorrhage cannot be told apart clinically and is excluded by the non-contrast CT, which matters here because he takes apixaban and aspirin. A unilateral leg deficit with incontinence can tempt a spinal diagnosis. Cauda equina syndrome gives back or radicular pain, saddle anaesthesia, retention with overflow and lower motor neurone signs. A cord lesion gives a sensory level, usually affects both legs, and in a hemicord (Brown-Séquard) lesion pain and temperature are lost on the opposite side. None of these fit Dominic. Other mimics are seizure with Todd's paresis, migraine with aura, infection, tumour and abscess.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: all in the white zone. This does not lower the urgency: the code stroke rests on the deficit and the time from onset. BP 158/92 is below 185/110.
  • Bloods: glucose excludes hypoglycaemia, and platelets and renal function are normal. A normal INR and APTT do not exclude an apixaban effect, so a drug-specific (apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa) level is needed.
  • ECG: AF with a controlled rate and no ischaemia.
  • CT: no haemorrhage, a right A2 occlusion, and on perfusion a small core (6 mL) with a large mismatch (36 mL): salvageable brain.

Acute management (Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines and the Acute Stroke Clinical Care Standard)

  • Activate the code stroke as soon as a sudden focal deficit within the treatment window is recognised. Get urgent non-contrast CT with CT angiography and perfusion, and check glucose.
  • Thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) is considered within 4.5 hours of onset. A DOAC taken within the previous 48 hours contraindicates it unless drug-specific testing shows no clinically relevant level, under the local protocol. Normal routine coagulation results are not enough. Dominic's last apixaban dose was about 14 hours before onset, so the decision rests with the stroke consultant and the apixaban level.
  • Endovascular clot retrieval is the standard of care for large vessel occlusion. An A2 occlusion is a medium vessel occlusion; the 2025 ESCAPE-MeVO and DISTAL trials showed no benefit from routine thrombectomy for these, so it is not standard care and is considered only case by case by the stroke and neurointervention team. Anticoagulation does not by itself rule out clot retrieval.
  • Blood pressure is not lowered routinely in the acute phase. If reperfusion therapy is given, keep it below 185/110 before treatment and below 180/105 afterwards.
  • Keep him nil by mouth, including oral medicines, until a swallow screen is passed. Give oxygen only if he is hypoxic. Monitor glucose and temperature, and treat hyperglycaemia and fever.
  • Withhold apixaban and aspirin for now. The stroke team decides when to restart anticoagulation, based on infarct size and bleeding risk. Cardiology reviews whether aspirin is still needed five years after his stent, because aspirin with an anticoagulant raises bleeding risk.
  • Admit to a stroke unit for multidisciplinary care (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech pathology, nursing). Use intermittent pneumatic compression for VTE prevention while he is immobile. Assess falls and pressure injury risk, and assess continence instead of placing a routine catheter.

Secondary prevention and safety netting

Secondary prevention means reliable long-term anticoagulation (twice-daily apixaban with adherence support), a statin, BP and diabetes control, quitting smoking and cocaine, a better diet, more exercise and weight loss. Dominic and his wife need the FAST message (Face, Arms, Speech, Time) and to call 000 at once for any new symptoms, even if they settle. On the ward, nurses escalate any neurological deterioration, new headache or vomiting (possible haemorrhagic transformation or swelling), BP outside the agreed limits, fever, or coughing with oral intake. Under Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive, a private driver should not drive for at least 4 weeks after a stroke (2 weeks after a TIA), and longer if deficits persist, until medically cleared. Follow-up includes rehabilitation, a stroke clinic, the GP, cardiology, and support for his wife as his carer.
points: A sudden focal deficit still present after an hour, with ischaemia on imaging, is a stroke, not a TIA. Earlier brief episodes in the same territory were TIAs and are warnings that need same-day assessment.
Leg weakness and sensory loss more than arm, with the face spared and urinary incontinence, localise to the contralateral anterior cerebral artery territory (paracentral lobule).
Establish the last known well time and the exact time of the last anticoagulant dose early, because both decide reperfusion eligibility.

A DOAC taken within 48 hours contraindicates thrombolysis unless a drug-specific level shows no relevant effect. A normal INR and APTT do not exclude apixaban. Clot retrieval is not ruled out by anticoagulation alone; for a medium vessel occlusion such as an A2 occlusion it is not routine and is decided case by case by the stroke team.

Check glucose in every suspected stroke, keep the patient nil by mouth (including tablets) until a swallow screen, and do not lower blood pressure routinely unless reperfusion therapy needs it below 185/110.
In AF, missed anticoagulant doses are a common and preventable cause of stroke. Address adherence without judgement, and teach FAST and calling 000 even if symptoms settle.
